title: Learning to Choose: Being Present Together
author: Jennifer W. Shewmaker and Julie Crum
summary: Jennifer Shewmaker and Julie Crum continue their Learning to Choose series on essential human skills by focusing on presence, the ability to give sustained attention to ideas, people and surroundings. Shewmaker opens with a graduate assessment course in which only a few students spoke up, and she realized the others could not yet see why the material mattered for their future clients. Her fix was to name presence explicitly and then structure practice for it: students voice their own why, hear practitioner stories, and get protected time for contemplative journaling and small-group talk. Crum shows how the same idea works in K-12, from a noticing walk for young students to a President's War Room simulation for secondary students, and from warm greetings by name to modeling belonging. The essay also asks where AI might let students bypass the attention that learning requires, offering before-and-after reflection prompts on whether AI helped or hindered presence. It closes with questions for teachers about whether they model presence or merely demand attention.
points: Presence has to be named and practiced rather than commanded, because telling students to pay attention does not show them what attention looks like.
Students invest attention when they can see the why, so having them voice their goals and hearing practitioner stories connects coursework to the people they will serve.
Active, student-led learning such as simulations, garden walks and read-alouds builds presence in ways a worksheet or an AI summary cannot.
Simple relational habits such as greeting students by name with eye contact help children feel known, which makes them more willing to engage.
Pre- and post-assignment AI reflection questions turn the decision to use AI into a conscious choice about what the student must notice for themselves.
quotes: Presence asks us to listen long enough to understand an idea and to ask questions when we are confused. It also asks us to stay engaged when the conversation becomes difficult.

For the students in my assessment class, I decided that they needed the opportunity to connect what they were learning in the course with the work they hoped to do in the future. In other words, they needed to understand the why behind learning this material.
What we’ve found is that the key is to be intentional in naming presence, why it matters, and explicitly providing the opportunity to practice it.

Instead of telling students to “Pay attention,” we can explain what that looks like. Young students might take a walk through the school, on the playground, or visit the school garden with the instructions to be super spies who are looking for details.

Oftentimes, teachers and school leaders can become overly focused on hitting academic benchmarks and goals to the point where we let distinctly human skills, such as the practice of presence, slide as we strive for better test scores. We are not programming machines, however.

Students who see presence modeled and are given the chance to practice it are more likely to practice it on their own. Children begin recognizing that belonging isn’t simply something we receive from a community. It’s also something we help create through our choices.

A student could learn about plants found in a learning garden from a computer. But it cannot replace the experience of kneeling in the dirt, touching the leaves, noticing the details, and sharing the wonder with a classmate.
